{{short description|Group of symmetries of the square}}
[[File:Animated symmetries of square.gif|thumb|alt=caption|The dihedral group of order 8 as the symmetry group of a [[square]]]]
In [[mathematics]], '''{{math|D{{sub|4}}}}''' (sometimes alternatively denoted by '''{{math|D{{sub|8}}}}''') is the [[dihedral group]] of [[degree (permutation group)|degree]] 4 and [[Order of a group|order]] 8. It is the [[symmetry group]] of a [[square]].<ref>{{cite book|first1=Bernard L. |last1=Johnston |first2=Fred |last2=Richman |year=1997 |title=Numbers and Symmetry: An Introduction to Algebra |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9780849303012 |page=92|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=koUfrlgsmUcC&pg=PA92}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Peter Jephson |last=Cameron |author-link=Peter Cameron (mathematician) |title=Introduction to Algebra |year=1998 |isbn=9780198501954 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=100|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=syYYl-NVM5IC&pg=PA100}}</ref> A square maintains its appearance under 90° rotations about its center (4-fold [[rotational symmetry]]), and under reflections across four lines passing through the center – two lines parallel to the sides and its two diagonals ([[reflection symmetry]]).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Krantz |first=Steven G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mMZBtxVZiQoC&pg=PA160 |title=The Proof is in the Pudding: The Changing Nature of Mathematical Proof |year=2011 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-48744-1 |page=160 |language=en}}</ref>

== Symmetries of a square ==
Consider a [[square]] of a certain thickness with the letter "F" written on it to make the different positions distinguishable. In order to describe its symmetry, one can form the set of all those rigid movements of the square that do not make a visible difference (except the "F"); each of these is a [[symmetry transformation]]. For instance, when the square is turned 90° clockwise or reflected across its vertical axis, it still looks the same, so these two movements are symmetry transformations.

Every point inside the square which does not lie on any of its four axes of symmetry will be mapped to 8 distinct points by these transformations, collectively called the point's ''[[Group action#Orbits and stabilizers|orbit]]''. An octant of the square (the region between one horizontal or vertical axis and one diagonal axis, an [[isosceles right triangle]]) is a [[fundamental domain]] of the square's surface under these symmetry transformations, containing one point from each possible orbit. One octant is highlighted in blue in the images above, to show how each symmetry transformation maps it onto a distinct octant.

=== Generating the group ===
[[File:Dih4 cycle graph.svg|thumb|right|[[Cycle graph (group)|Cycle graph]] of Dih<sub>4</sub><br/>''a'' is the clockwise rotation<br/>and ''b'' the horizontal reflection.]]
[[File:Dih 4 Cayley Graph; generators a, b.svg|thumb|[[Cayley graph]] of Dih<sub>4</sub>]]
[[File:Dih 4 Cayley Graph; generators b, c.svg|thumb|A different Cayley graph of Dih<sub>4</sub>, generated by the horizontal reflection ''b'' and a diagonal reflection ''c'']]

With [[function composition|composition]] as the operation, the set of all those movements forms a [[Group (mathematics)|group]]: Applying two symmetry transformations in succession yields a symmetry transformation, so the transformations are ''closed'' under composition. The symmetries of the square can be fully described by this group's [[Cayley table]], analogous to a multiplication table but using the group operation instead of multiplication. To draw such a table explicitly, each symmetry must be assigned some symbol. In the following table, each symmetry is represented concretely by a curved arrow (rotation), double-ended arrow (reflection), or dot (identity transformation), corresponding to the images above:

Each entry in this table represents the composition of two symmetries: that is, the symmetry transformation resulting from performing first the symmetry transformation for the column and then performing the symmetry transformation for the row. For instance, a reflection in the diagonal NE–SW direction {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png|frameless|22px]])}} followed by a horizontal reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]])}} is equivalent to a three-quarters-turn rotation anticlockwise {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png|frameless|22px]]),}} which can be written as an equation {{nobr|[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]] <math>\circ</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png|frameless|22px]] <math>=</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]]}}, using the convention that <math>x \circ y</math> means applying {{tmath|x}} after {{tmath|y}}. Thus the table entry for row [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]] and column [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png|frameless|22px]] is [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]].

Instead of pictorial symbols, mathematicians more commonly use letters. The [[Juxtaposition#Mathematics|juxtaposition]] of two letters {{tmath|xy}} represents the composition of their respective symmetries {{tmath|x \circ y}}, and an integer [[superscript]] represents the composition of the same symmetry multiple times, e.g. {{tmath|x^3}} represents {{tmath|x \circ x \circ x }} and {{tmath|x^{-1} }} represents the inverse of {{tmath|x}}. The letter {{tmath|e}} is commonly used for the identity element. The use of this shorthand reduces the number of distinct symbols required to represent group elements.

Any element which can be written as the composition of a particular set of elements is said to be ''generated'' by those elements, for example the element {{tmath|1= x^2yx = x \circ x \circ y \circ x}} is generated by {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}}; any set of elements which generates the whole group is called a [[Generating set of a group|generating set of the group]]. Every dihedral group can be generated from two elements, so only three elements of the group (those two and the identity) need be assigned symbols, and the other elements can be expressed by combining them.

The symmetries of the square can be generated in two basic ways: using one diagonal reflection and one horizontal or vertical reflection, or using one quarter-turn rotation and one reflection. For example, letting the letter {{tmath|r}} represent a quarter-turn rotation anticlockwise {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]])}}, letting the letter {{tmath|v}} represent a vertical reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]])}}, and letting the letter {{tmath|d}} represent a diagonal NW–SE reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]])}}, any pair of these elements generates the group, and the rest of the group elements can be written in terms of these. Concretely, each symmetry could be written as any of the following (the various expressions in each row represent the same symmetry):

Two elements {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} are ''conjugate'' to each-other if there is an element {{tmath|g}} such that {{tmath|1= x = gyg^{-1} }}. The set of all elements which are pairwise conjugate is called a ''[[conjugacy class]]''. These classes are important because two elements which are conjugate to each-other cannot be distinguished using only the group structure. The dihedral group of order 8 has 5 [[Conjugacy class|conjugacy classes]]:
{{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>}},
{{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>}},
{{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>}},
{{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>}},
{{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>}}.

In mathematics this group is known as the '''[[dihedral group]]''' of order 8, and is either denoted Dih<sub>4</sub>, D<sub>4</sub> or D<sub>8</sub>, depending on the convention. 
This is an example of a [[non-abelian group]]: the operation <math>\circ</math> here is not [[commutative]], which can be seen from the table; the table is not symmetrical about the main diagonal.

There are five different groups of order 8. Three of them are abelian: the [[cyclic group]] ''C''<sub>8</sub> and the [[Direct product of groups|direct products]] of cyclic groups ''C''<sub>4</sub>×''C''<sub>2</sub> and ''C''<sub>2</sub>×''C''<sub>2</sub>×''C''<sub>2</sub>. The other two, the dihedral group of order 8 and the [[quaternion group]], are not.<ref>{{cite book|first=J. F. |last=Humphreys |title=A Course in Group Theory |year=1996 |isbn=9780198534594 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=47}}</ref>

===Permutation representation===
[[File:Dihedral group of order 8; Cayley table (element orders 1,2,2,4,2,2,4,2); subgroup of S4.svg|thumb|{{math|D{{sub|4}}}} is isomorphic to the permutation group generated by {{math|(1234)}} and {{math|(13)}}, a subgroup of {{math|S{{sub|4}}}}. The numbers in this table come from numbering the {{math|1= 4! = 24}} elements of {{math|S{{sub|4}}}} from {{math|0}} (shown as a black circle) to {{math|23}}.]]
Every symmetry transformation of the square permutes (re-orders) the square's four corners, so each symmetry transformation can be associated to a particular [[permutation]] of four elements; therefore {{tmath|\mathrm{D}_4}} is [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to a [[permutation group]], a subgroup of the [[symmetric group]] {{tmath|\mathrm{S}_4}} of all permutations of {{math|4}} elements.

If the corners of a square are numbered consecutively, starting from 1 in the upper right and proceeding counterclockwise, then the permutation corresponding to each symmetry transformation can be written using [[cycle notation]]:

===Matrix representation===

Symmetry transformations of an axis-aligned square centered at the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] are [[linear transformation]]s, so can be [[Group representation|represented]] by [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] acting on the plane by multiplication on [[column vector]]s of coordinates <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}x\\y\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math>. Specifically, these transformations correspond to [[signed permutation matrix|signed permutation matrices]].

The identity transformation {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by the [[identity matrix]] <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math>.
A horizontal reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by the matrix <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math> which negates the {{tmath|x}} coordinate, while a vertical reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by the matrix <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math> which negates the {{tmath|y}} coordinate. The NW–SE diagonal reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by the matrix <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math> which exchanges the two coordinates, while the NE–SW diagonal reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by its negative {{nobr|<math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math>.}} A rotation anticlockwise by a quarter turn {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]])}} is represented by the matrix {{nobr|<math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math>,}} and a rotation by three quarters of a turn {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]])}} by its negative {{nobr|<math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math>.}} Finally, a rotation by a half-turn {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]])}}, equivalent to a [[Point reflection|reflection across the center point]], is represented by the matrix <math>\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]</math> which negates both coordinates. The group composition operation is represented as [[matrix multiplication]].

Four of these matrices, representing for example the identity transformation, a vertical reflection, a diagonal reflection, and a quarter-turn rotation, form a [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for the [[matrix algebra]] {{tmath|\mathrm{M}_2(\R)}} of {{tmath|2 \times 2}} real matrices.

Larger signed permutation matrices represent in the same way the [[hyperoctahedral group]]s, the groups of symmetries of higher dimensional cubes, [[Regular octahedron|octahedra]], [[hypercube]]s, and [[cross polytope]]s.<ref>{{cite conference
 | last1 = Estévez | first1 = Manuel
 | last2 = Roldán | first2 = Érika
 | last3 = Segerman | first3 = Henry | author3-link = Henry Segerman
 | editor1-last = Holdener | editor1-first = Judy | editor1-link = Judy Holdener
 | editor2-last = Torrence | editor2-first = Eve | editor2-link = Eve Torrence
 | editor3-last = Fong | editor3-first = Chamberlain
 | editor4-last = Seaton | editor4-first = Katherine
 | arxiv = 2311.06596
 | contribution = Surfaces in the tesseract

 | year = 2023}}</ref>

=== Split-quaternions ===

The [[split-quaternions]] are a number-like algebraic structure with four dimensions, similar to the [[quaternions]]. Like the quaternions, their multiplication is [[associative]] but not [[commutative]].

They can be written in terms of four basis elements <math>\{1, i, j, k\}</math> which satisfy the basic identities:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
i^2 &= -1, & ij &= -ji = k, \\
j^2 &= 1, & jk &= -kj = -i, \\
k^2 &= 1, & ki &= -ik = j.
\end{align}</math>

The group of these basis elements and their negatives, with multiplication as the group operation, is isomorphic to the dihedral group {{tmath|\mathrm{D}_4}}, where {{tmath|1}} corresponds to the identity transformation {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]])}}, {{tmath|i}} corresponds to a quarter-turn rotation {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]])}}, {{tmath|j}} corresponds to a vertical reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]])}}, and {{tmath|k}} corresponds to a diagonal reflection {{nobr|([[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]])}}. ==Subgroups==
[[File:Dih4 subgroups.svg|thumb|Subgroups of D4]]
A [[subgroup]] of a group is a [[subset]] of the elements which also form a group. {{math|D{{sub|4}}}} has three subgroups of order four: one consisting of the four rotations of the square by quarter turns {{nobr|(<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>)}} which is a [[cyclic group]] of order 4, and two others generated by pairs of perpendicular reflections {{nobr|(<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>
}} and {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>)}} each of which is a dihedral group {{math|D{{sub|2}}}} (also known as the [[Klein four-group]]). Each of the four reflections generates a cyclic subgroup of order 2 {{nobr|(<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>,
}} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>,
}} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, and
}} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math>
[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>)}}. One final cyclic subgroup of order 2 consists of the rotations by half-turns {{nobr|(<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>).
}}

For every subgroup {{math|''H''}} in {{math|D{{sub|4}}}}, the group can be split into a collection of disjoint subsets of the same size (cardinality) as  {{math|''H''}}, called ''[[coset]]s''. There are both left cosets, of the form <math>gH = \{\, g \circ h \mid h \in H \,\}</math> and right cosets, sets of the form {{nobr|<math>Hg = \{\, h\circ g \mid h \in H \,\}\!</math>.}} For example, the subgroup {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>,}} has four left cosets,
{{bi|left=1.6| {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} and {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} }}
and four right cosets,
{{bi|left=1.6| {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – I.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – V.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R1.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – D2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R3.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>, }} and {{nobr|<math>\{</math>[[File:D4 symmetry symbol – H.png |frameless|22px]]<math>,</math> [[File:D4 symmetry symbol – R2.png |frameless|22px]]<math>\}</math>. }} }}

=== Normal subgroups ===
A subgroup is called ''[[normal subgroup|normal]]'' if it contains all of the conjugates of its elements. Both of the groups of rotations, as well as the dihedral groups of order 4, are normal subgroups. The four subgroups generated by a single reflection are not normal.

For a normal subgroup, the left and right cosets coincide, and the cosets themselves form a [[quotient group]].

This version of the Cayley table shows one of these normal subgroups, shown with a red background. In this table r means rotations, and f means flips. Because this subgroup is normal, the left coset is the same as the right coset.
